story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built Connecting Captions, a live captioning and translation overlay for macOS that runs entirely on-device. Nothing goes over the network: no API calls, no audio leaving your machine, and it keeps working offline.

I wanted live translation I could use in meetings and conversations without worrying about connectivity, latency spikes, or sending sensitive audio to a third party.

The technically interesting part is a low-latency, self-correcting pipeline for speech-to-text and translation. It has two modes:

Sentence mode: buffers until a sentence boundary, then translates with full context. It’s more accurate, especially between languages with different word order. Streaming mode: translates word by word as speech arrives, trading grammatical accuracy for minimal delay.

Current state:

Platform: macOS Models: Whisper Latency: ~200 ms Languages: 25

Code: https://github.com/chrisswimlee/connectingCaptions

I’d love feedback, especially on the self-correction approach and which use cases matter most to people.

title.value: Show HN: Connecting Captions Local Private AI Interpreter

story_text.value:
At a dinner party with other parents recently, the conversation turned to the challenges we all have with communication coming from our children's schools. Emails and Texts and App notifications, coming from Teachers, Admins, PTA, After-Care programs. Overlapping information, buried key details, verbose fluff. An avalanche of text every day that must be carefully parsed to find important info.

This seems to be a universal problem and certainly one I experience every day. So literally before dinner was over I built the first version of this site on my phone with Claude.

I think the main problem is that the folks who are responsible for communication just don't have the tools and experience to know what good communication really looks like, or the parents perspective hasn't been demonstrated to them to give them more empathy. So I am hoping this can help. Feel free to share if you have the same problem with your school.

title.value: Show HN: Parents Inbox – Communication Guide for Schools

story_text.value:
Lately I've been testing frontier models by having them create self-contained web pages that display clocks--sort of my personal version of Simon Willison’s pelican-on-a-bicycle metric.

I have been particularly impressed by the variety, interest, and quality of the clocks created by Claude Opus 5.5. Over the course of several sessions in the Claude chat interface, I had it build a total of 500 clocks.

Claude’s summary of the prompting process and page design is here:

https://github.com/tkgally/500-clocks/tree/main

story_text.value:
Hi everyone,

This started as an exploration into harnesses and locally hostable LLMs (the kind that uses less power than a small electric heater), and I used it as an opportunity to retool. I've tried popular ones like Cline, Claude Code, and Pi, but wanted a different UX and integrated sandboxes.

The solution that I've landed on is a responsive web interface where I can quickly drive progress. It feels like a microcosm of my day job: define and delegate tasks, organize using kanban, then review deliverables. And it also feels like the time I used to spend coding is now spent in code review with the agent, so I tried to optimize the UX to make review feel nicer.

One of my (maybe a bit niche) benchmark use-cases is how pleasant it is to make progress on hobby software projects while also out on a hike. This meant specifying low bandwidth usage and offline mode.

Now I can jot down an idea, start the task, and at some point down the trail: get a notification* that either clarification is needed, a decision needs to be made, or the code is ready for review. I've been having a good time with this.

To build MIKE, I exclusively used locally hostable LLMs (from Google, Meta, Qwen, Poolside, and DeepSeek) hosted with llama.cpp on my machines at home (Strix Halo and a 5090) to "compile" the code. The experience has gotten substantially better ever since DeepSeek’s release in July. Side note: I have a soft spot for llama.cpp since it was one of the first that made it possible to run this new tech at home, and its maintainers accepted a tiny improvement I made to error reporting. Oh the joys of having a PR get approved.

I plan on maintaining this, at least until similar features are supported by better tools. Until then, hope you find this useful!

5 minute demo: https://youtu.be/jexzLkZ50FU

p.s.

I didn't mention details about the sandbox earlier since most people seem to find this a bit boring. It was one of my critical requirements, and I opted to use an existing battle-tested sandbox. I'm not an expert on how the Linux kernel works, but seeing all the VM escape exploits recently is a bit scary, and I liked gVisor’s approach to the problem.

I'm also using Git worktrees to provision the agent’s workspace, as well as a read-only repository mount to provide relevant context when the agent looks for it.

*off by default

title.value: Show HN: Cosplay as a tech lead, using gVisor to sandbox agents

story_text.value:
I’ve been working on a Nix CSI for kubernetes since NixCon when I realized that everyone seems to working towards killing OCI layers (and images) in Kubernetes deployments.

I’m hoping to get people to give it a spin and report back to me bugs, feature requests or general feedback. I don’t have a lot of data on how this scales and that makes it hard to decide whether to justify adding a feature or not (e.g. cache locality scheduling).

An LLM was used in the development of this project.
